strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem in multimodal document retrieval: improving the performance-efficiency tradeoff of ColPali-style visual retrievers without scaling document representations further.

The proposed Guided Query Refinement method is simple, modular, and practically appealing: it refines only the query representation at test time using a complementary retriever's score distribution, so it can be applied across single-vector and multi-vector retrievers without training a new model.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad for the target subarea, covering ViDoRe 1 and ViDoRe 2, three vision-centric retrievers, three text-centric retrievers, multiple hybrid retrieval baselines, Recall@5/NDCG@5, latency, memory, and reranker comparisons.

The main ViDoRe 2 results are consistent: GQR improves all three multimodal base retrievers on average, with especially meaningful gains for Jina vision and Colnomic, and it compares favorably to tuned score fusion on average.

The efficiency analysis is a real strength. The paper makes a plausible case that Colnomic or Jina with GQR reaches a better latency/memory-quality regime than much larger late-interaction models and substantially faster than cross-encoder reranking pipelines.

The appendices include useful design-choice analyses, including candidate-pool policy, extra search after query refinement, alternative losses, role swapping between primary and complementary models, and additional Recall@5 results.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than strong. GQR is closely related to prior test-time query optimization and pseudo-relevance feedback methods; the main change is replacing a cross-encoder signal with a complementary bi-encoder/multimodal retriever. This is useful, but the paper could position more sharply what is conceptually new beyond adapting existing query-refinement ideas to multimodal hybrid retrieval.

The gains are meaningful but modest. On ViDoRe 2, the average gain over tuned score aggregation is small, and on ViDoRe 1 the method is essentially neutral due to benchmark saturation. This makes the contribution more incremental than transformative.

The comparison to hybrid baselines is somewhat limited. The paper compares rank and score aggregation variants, but does not include some potentially strong alternatives such as learned lightweight fusion, query-adaptive fusion without LLMs, calibration-based score normalization, BM25/OCR lexical fusion, or distillation/training-time alignment baselines.

The latency and memory claims need more careful accounting. The headline 14x faster and 54x lower-memory comparisons are against a different larger base retriever, while GQR itself requires an additional retriever/index and iterative optimization. The memory table appears to underemphasize or inconsistently account for complementary text-index storage, especially for Jina text, and the hardware/indexing setup is not described in enough detail to fully interpret deployment costs.

The method is evaluated only on visual document retrieval benchmarks. The paper claims architecture-agnostic and broadly useful hybrid retrieval behavior, but does not test non-visual retrieval, larger corpora, out-of-domain transfer, or realistic production-scale indexes where candidate generation, caching, and approximate search behavior may change the tradeoffs.

There is no statistical reliability analysis. Prompt-free retrieval models are less stochastic than LLM prompting, but the benchmarks and sampled latency measurements would still benefit from confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or bootstrap estimates, especially because several improvements are small.

The optimization objective is underspecified. Since the consensus distribution includes the current primary distribution, it is important to state whether gradients flow through the consensus term or whether it is detached; the mathematical description and intuition could otherwise imply different objectives.

The method depends on an in-domain development set for tuning learning rate and iteration count per subset, which weakens the zero-shot practicality story and may inflate benchmark-specific performance. More analysis of sensitivity to hyperparameters and performance under a single global setting would strengthen the evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript. The abstract says code is released but the URL is missing, and several details such as exact model checkpoints, indexing libraries, approximate search settings, batch sizes, precision, optimizer settings beyond Adam, and latency measurement protocol need to be more explicit.

The paper would benefit from a deeper error analysis. It shows average gains, but does not characterize which queries benefit, when weaker text retrievers misguide the visual retriever, or whether improvements mainly come from reordering the union candidate pool rather than genuinely improving representation-level matching.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant problem: improving efficiency-performance tradeoffs for visual document retrieval with multimodal late-interaction retrievers.
The proposed GQR procedure is clearly described at a high level and is modular: it can in principle be applied to heterogeneous retriever pairs without training a new fusion model.

The empirical comparison includes multiple recent vision and text retrievers, several standard hybrid fusion baselines, latency measurements, memory estimates, recall results, and some design-choice ablations.

On ViDoRe 2, the reported gains over the primary retriever and over standard rank/score fusion baselines are consistent in the aggregate, and the method appears especially useful for reordering a small candidate pool.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. GQR is essentially test-time query embedding optimization using another retriever's score distribution as pseudo-feedback, closely related to prior query-refinement and relevance-feedback methods; the multimodal/hybrid setting is useful but not a major conceptual advance.

The central efficiency claims are not fully convincing. The memory accounting appears to focus on per-document index storage and does not clearly include all costs of maintaining and serving the complementary retriever, model memory, OCR/text-indexing overhead, or system-level deployment costs. The headline 14x/54x comparison is selective against a much heavier baseline.

The evaluation is narrow and benchmark-dependent. Main positive results are concentrated on ViDoRe 2, while ViDoRe 1 shows essentially no meaningful gain over strong primary retrievers. There is no evaluation on broader retrieval settings, larger corpora, out-of-domain queries, or non-visual-document benchmarks to substantiate architecture-agnostic claims.

The experimental protocol raises concerns. The method requires in-domain development queries for tuning T and learning rate, but the tables are labeled with 'val' columns and the paper is not fully clear about held-out test separation, repeated tuning, or possible benchmark overfitting.

The improvements over strong tuned score-fusion baselines are modest. For ViDoRe 2, GQR averages 3.9% gain while tuned min-max score aggregation gives 3.4%; this small margin needs statistical significance testing, per-query analysis, and robustness checks, none of which are provided.

The method's mechanism seems largely limited to reranking the union of initial top-K results. The paper itself reports that an extra full-index search after query refinement provides no improvement, weakening the claim that GQR meaningfully exploits representation-level retrieval beyond candidate reordering.

Important ablations are missing or underdeveloped: sensitivity to K, number of optimization steps, learning rate, optimizer choice, candidate-pool size, score temperature/calibration, and failure cases where the complementary retriever misleads the primary retriever.

The reranker comparison is not strong enough. It uses one open multimodal reranker and a limited setup; stronger or better-tuned rerankers, distilled rerankers, and efficient late-interaction indexing systems would be necessary to support broad Pareto-frontier claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code will be released but the URL is missing, and implementation details for latency measurement, indexing backend, hardware utilization, batching, OCR settings, and exact splits are insufficient for confident reproduction.

The writing and presentation have polish issues, including a dangling code-release sentence, some cramped tables, inconsistent capitalization/model names, and broad claims such as 'state-of-the-art' and 'Pareto frontier' that are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: Clear and timely problem: improving the quality-efficiency tradeoff for visual document retrieval is important, and the paper targets a concrete deployment bottleneck of large late-interaction multimodal retrievers.

The proposed Guided Query Refinement method is simple, architecture-agnostic, and practically appealing: it uses a complementary retriever’s score distribution to refine the primary query embedding at test time without training a new model.

The evaluation is reasonably broad for this subarea, covering ViDoRe 1 and ViDoRe 2, three multimodal primary retrievers, three text retrievers, multiple rank/score fusion baselines, recall results, latency/memory analysis, reranker comparisons, and several design ablations.

The empirical results are consistently positive on ViDoRe 2, with useful gains over base multimodal retrievers and a compelling Pareto-frontier story: smaller Colnomic/Jina-based systems with GQR can approach or exceed much larger Llama-Nemo retrieval quality at far lower latency and storage cost.
The paper is well written and well organized, with clear motivation, an understandable algorithm, and helpful tables/figures for performance-efficiency tradeoffs.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. GQR is closely related to prior test-time query representation optimization and pseudo-relevance feedback methods; the main contribution is a useful adaptation to multimodal hybrid retrieval rather than a fundamentally new retrieval paradigm.

The improvement over the strongest tuned score-fusion baselines is small in the averaged ViDoRe 2 tables: e.g., GQR NDCG@5 62.3 vs. tuned Min-Max score aggregation 62.1, and Recall@5 58.6 vs. 58.5. This weakens the claim that representation-level refinement is substantially better than well-tuned score-level fusion.

The method relies on an in-domain development set and tunes hyperparameters per subset. This is acknowledged, but it makes the results less clearly zero-shot/practical and raises some concern that small gains over tuned baselines may be sensitive to split choice.

There are no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals. Given that several gains are small and some subset/model combinations degrade, it is difficult to judge robustness beyond the reported averages.

ViDoRe 1 shows essentially no improvement over the strong primary retrievers, and the authors attribute this to saturation. That is plausible, but it also means the main evidence for effectiveness rests heavily on ViDoRe 2.

The method only reranks/refines within a small candidate pool by default; the extra full-index search ablation shows little benefit, but the paper could more deeply analyze failure cases where the relevant document is absent from the initial union pool.

Reproducibility is decent but incomplete from the manuscript alone: exact development/test splits, full implementation details for efficient gradient refinement over multi-vector retrievers, and the promised code link appear underspecified or missing in the anonymized text.

strengths: Clear and timely problem: improving the efficiency-quality tradeoff for visual document retrieval is important, and the paper targets a practical bottleneck in ColPali-style multi-vector retrievers.

The proposed GQR method is simple, architecture-agnostic, and practically appealing: it refines only the query representation at test time using a complementary retriever’s score distribution, avoiding expensive model retraining.

Evaluation is fairly broad, covering multiple ViDoRe benchmarks, three multimodal retrievers, three text retrievers, several hybrid baselines, latency/memory analysis, reranker comparison, and ablations on candidate pool, extra search, and loss choice.

Results are consistently positive on ViDoRe 2 and ViDoRe 3, with especially compelling efficiency comparisons showing smaller multimodal models plus GQR approaching or exceeding much larger late-interaction models at substantially lower latency and storage.
The paper is well organized and generally clear, with useful appendix details on model sizes, hyperparameters, recall metrics, and additional benchmark tables.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. GQR is closely related to test-time query optimization and distribution matching/pseudo-relevance feedback; the main novelty is adapting this idea to hybrid multimodal retrieval with a lightweight complementary retriever rather than introducing a fundamentally new retrieval principle.

The claim of representation-level hybrid retrieval is somewhat overstated. The guidance signal is still based on score distributions over a top-K candidate pool, and the method functions primarily as candidate reranking rather than true full-corpus retrieval refinement.

The strongest tuned results depend on substantial per-subset and per-model hyperparameter selection for learning rate and optimization steps. This raises concerns about how robust GQR is under realistic deployment without validation labels, even though the ViDoRe 3 zero-shot experiment partially mitigates this.

The gains, while consistent, are often modest in absolute NDCG, and ViDoRe 1 appears saturated. The paper would benefit from statistical significance testing or confidence intervals to establish whether small differences over tuned score-fusion baselines are reliable.

Efficiency claims are promising but not fully stress-tested. Latency is measured on a single A100 and small benchmark settings; large-scale ANN/index traversal behavior, batching effects, CPU/GPU memory pressure, and the overhead of maintaining the complementary text pipeline are not deeply analyzed.

The memory comparison may understate total deployment cost because GQR requires an additional complementary index and, for text retrievers, OCR/markdown/text ingestion. The headline comparisons to Llama-Nemo are useful but should more explicitly include full-system storage and preprocessing assumptions.

Baseline coverage is good but still leaves gaps: stronger or more diverse rerankers, dynamic/query-adaptive fusion, pseudo-relevance feedback baselines, BM25/OCR hybrids, and learned lightweight fusion methods would make the empirical case more decisive.

The method is evaluated only in visual document retrieval. The architecture-agnostic framing would be stronger with evidence on another retrieval domain or at least a discussion of when the method is expected to fail, for example when the complementary retriever is highly correlated or systematically misaligned.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in multimodal/visual document retrieval: improving the quality-efficiency tradeoff of late-interaction vision-centric retrievers.

Guided Query Refinement is simple, architecture-agnostic in principle, and intuitively motivated as a way to use a complementary retriever without directly overriding the primary retriever's scoring space.

The empirical section covers several strong recent vision and text retrievers, multiple ViDoRe benchmark versions, and compares against ranking-level, score-level, tuned, and zero-shot hybrid retrieval baselines.
The paper includes useful efficiency measurements, including latency and storage comparisons, and the results suggest GQR can move some systems closer to the latency-performance Pareto frontier.
The appendix contains several relevant design checks, including candidate-pool variants, extra-search variants, loss-function variants, Recall@5 results, and role-swapping experiments.
weaknesses: The main empirical advantage over strong tuned score-fusion baselines is very small. On ViDoRe 2, GQR averages 62.3 NDCG@5 versus 62.1 for tuned min-max score aggregation, and on ViDoRe 3 the gain over tuned min-max is similarly modest. This makes the central claim of a substantially better hybrid method under-supported.

The claimed comparison to much larger representation models is fragile: Colnomic+GQR only approximately matches or barely exceeds Llama-Nemo without reported statistical significance, while Llama-Nemo+GQR remains better. The paper leans heavily on tiny absolute differences without confidence intervals, randomization tests, or query-level significance analysis.

The novelty is limited. Test-time query embedding optimization with pseudo-feedback is known, and this paper mainly substitutes a complementary bi-encoder for a reranker/cross-encoder in a multimodal retrieval setting. The conceptual step is useful but not clearly strong enough for a top-tier contribution without more compelling evidence.

The method is not truly end-to-end retrieval after refinement in the main setting: it mostly reranks the union of two top-K lists, and the extra search stage provides no benefit. This weakens the representation-level retrieval framing and makes the method closer to a learned/test-time reranking procedure over a small candidate pool.

The evaluation depends on substantial hyperparameter tuning per subset and model pair for ViDoRe 1/2. This raises concerns about robustness and practical deployability, especially since the method is sensitive to learning rate and optimization steps.

The comparison to reranking is incomplete. Top-10 and top-20 rerankers outperform GQR in quality, albeit with higher latency, but the discussion emphasizes Pareto efficiency without deeply analyzing whether GQR's lower quality is acceptable or whether stronger/faster rerankers would change the conclusion.

The paper lacks deeper failure analysis. It shows aggregate gains but gives little insight into which query/document types benefit, when weak complementary retrievers hurt, how OCR/verbalization quality affects the method, or why certain subsets show much larger improvements.

Reproducibility details are only partial. Important implementation choices such as whether gradients flow through the consensus target, exact indexing/search settings, hardware utilization, batching, and code/data availability are not specified clearly enough to make the reported latency and quality numbers easy to reproduce.

The presentation sometimes overstates the contribution relative to the evidence, especially claims about exploiting rich representation-level interactions and pushing the Pareto frontier, given that the strongest gains over tuned score fusion are marginal.

strengths: Clear and timely contribution: Guided Query Refinement is a simple, architecture-agnostic test-time method for hybrid multimodal retrieval that operates more richly than rank- or score-level fusion while preserving modularity.

Strong empirical coverage: the paper evaluates multiple vision-centric and text-centric retrievers, nine model pairs on ViDoRe 1/2, zero-shot transfer to ViDoRe 3, and compares against rank fusion, score fusion, tuned fusion, and a multimodal reranker.

The performance-efficiency story is compelling: GQR gives consistent gains on ViDoRe 2 and ViDoRe 3 and shows favorable latency and storage tradeoffs, including matching or exceeding much heavier late-interaction models with substantially lower query latency and memory.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses, including hyperparameter sweeps, latency breakdowns, candidate-pool variants, extra search, alternative losses, role swapping, Recall@5, and per-query dynamics.
The method is well motivated and clearly explained, with a coherent connection to hybrid retrieval and test-time query optimization literature.
weaknesses: Novelty is meaningful but not radical: the method is closely related to prior test-time query optimization and pseudo-relevance feedback, with the main contribution being a practical adaptation to multimodal hybrid retrieval using a complementary bi-encoder signal.

The gains over strong tuned score-fusion baselines are positive but sometimes modest, e.g. average improvements over tuned score aggregation are small on ViDoRe 2 and ViDoRe 3, so some of the impact rests on efficiency rather than large quality gains.

The tuned setting uses an in-domain 10% development split per subset and tunes GQR hyperparameters per subset/model pair, which may overstate practical robustness; the zero-shot ViDoRe 3 results help but do not fully remove this concern.
There is no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals, which matters because several reported differences between GQR and tuned score-fusion baselines are small.

The evaluation is focused on ViDoRe-style visual document retrieval; evidence for generality beyond this benchmark family, larger production-scale corpora, or non-document multimodal retrieval settings is limited.

Some reproducibility details are still underspecified, including the exact code release location, full indexing/search implementation details, and whether latency measurements include all relevant production overheads under comparable hardware and batching assumptions.
